title: Reality Is the Final Auditor
author: Killian, Eddie
summary: Eddie Killian develops a framework for diagnosing organizational failure long before it becomes visible on a financial statement, arguing that annual-report measures like revenue and margin are taken 'near the end of a journey' and can be perfectly accurate while the underlying interpretation is wrong. His central diagnostic question — 'where did the energy go?' — asks readers to trace labor, electricity, machinery, attention, and time through an institution rather than trusting output metrics alone, paired with a parallel information flow that must travel from a frontline observation (a mechanic hearing an unfamiliar vibration) up through a hierarchy to someone with the authority to act. Killian's key mechanism for why organizations fail to correct themselves despite nobody lying is compression: each layer of hierarchy restates a problem in blander, more generic language (a vibration becomes 'a developing reliability concern' becomes 'the issue is being managed'), and each restatement loses information even though everyone in the chain behaves reasonably within their own role. He names a further failure mode in which a single exceptional employee's competence compensates for a broken process, which conceals the defect from leadership until that employee leaves and the resulting collapse gets misdiagnosed as a staffing problem. The essay culminates in his proposed role for an outside diagnostician — literally seated in 'the dark corner of the boardroom' — whose only job is to notice where different departments' honest answers stop fitting together and ask 'what are we missing,' under a philosophy he calls Structural Coherence Realism, built on the claim that systems endure in proportion to the truth they can process in time.
points: Killian argues financial statements are measurements taken 'near the end of a journey' that can be perfectly accurate while the underlying interpretation is wrong, such as when output rises because deferred equipment maintenance or absorbed unpaid overtime is masking real capability loss.

His central diagnostic question, 'where did the energy go,' asks an observer to trace labor, electricity, machinery, attention, and time through an institution rather than trusting revenue or margin alone.

The mechanism he identifies for silent organizational failure is linguistic compression through hierarchy: a mechanic's specific vibration becomes a 'developing reliability concern,' then 'the issue is being managed,' with real information lost at each restatement even though nobody in the chain lied.

He names a distinct failure mode in which an exceptional employee's competence quietly compensates for a defective process, concealing the defect from leadership until that employee leaves, at which point the resulting collapse gets misdiagnosed as a staffing shortage.

His proposed remedy is a designated outside diagnostician seated apart from the table ('the dark corner of the boardroom') whose sole job is to notice where different departments' honest, siloed answers stop fitting together and ask 'what are we missing.'
quotes: There is a moment in the life of a failing organization when almost everyone inside it still believes it is working.

The financial statement tells us a great deal about what emerged. It cannot always tell us what was consumed along the way. A company can increase output by asking more of equipment whose maintenance has been deferred.

A worker says the machine will fail. The supervisor reports a developing reliability concern. The manager writes that Maintenance is monitoring an emerging condition. The director tells the executive team that the issue is being managed. Nobody has lied, yet something has disappeared.

Exceptional people can keep defective structures alive long enough to convince leadership that the structures work. When the exceptional person leaves, the organization often calls what follows a staffing problem.

Good intentions cannot repeal causality. Concrete cracks whether money exists for the repair. Customers leave despite favorable satisfaction scores. Reality does not participate in the meeting, negotiate with the forecast, or care who approved the plan. Eventually it sends the invoice.
I am not the final auditor. Neither is the CEO, the board, the consultant, the regulator, the market, the professor, or the expert. My ambition is simply to arrive a little earlier.
